specStatements.text: When a current flows through a conducting wire a magnetic field is produced around the wire. The strength of the magnetic field depends on the current through the wire and the distance from the wire.
Shaping a wire to form a solenoid increases the strength of the magnetic field created by a current through the wire. The magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform.

The magnetic field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet. Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid. An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core.
Students should be able to:
• describe how the magnetic effect of a current can be demonstrated
• draw the magnetic field pattern for a straight wire carrying a current and for a solenoid (showing the direction of the field)
• explain how a solenoid arrangement can increase the magnetic effect of the current.
(Physics only) Students should be able to interpret diagrams of electromagnetic devices in order to explain how they work.
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.
Students should be able to show that Fleming's left-hand rule represents the relative orientation of the force, the current in the conductor and the magnetic field.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the size of the force on the conductor.
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current:
force = magnetic flux density × current × length
[F = B I l]
force, F, in newtons, N
magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
length, l, in metres, m
A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate. This is the basis of an electric motor.
Students should be able to explain how t he force on a conductor in a magnetic field causes the rotation of the coil in an electric motor.

scopeNotes.statement: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This clause fixes the condition under which F = B I l may be used, so it is honoured as a boundary rather than tested for its own sake. Both calculations in this content (q20, q21) state explicitly that the conductor is at right angles to the field, and no item asks for the force at an intermediate angle. The single item dealing with a conductor lying along the field (q16) states only that the force is then zero; no version of the equation containing a sine or cosine factor, and no resolving of a field into components, appears anywhere in this material.

concepts.definition: Whenever a current flows in a conducting wire, a magnetic field is produced in the space around the wire. The field exists only while the current flows: switch the current off and the field disappears.

concepts.term: Field pattern around a straight wire
concepts.definition: The field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles lying in a plane at right angles to the wire and centred on it. The circles are drawn close together near the wire and further apart further away, showing that the field is strongest close to the wire.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the field around a wire
concepts.definition: The strength of the magnetic field around a wire depends on two things: the current through the wire, and the distance from the wire. A larger current gives a stronger field; moving further from the wire gives a weaker field.

concepts.term: Direction of the field around a wire
concepts.definition: The direction of the circular field lines is shown by arrowheads and is given by the right-hand grip rule: point the right thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. Reversing the current reverses every arrow.

A solenoid is a wire wound into a long coil of many turns. Shaping the wire this way increases the strength of the magnetic field produced by a given current, because the field of each turn adds to the field of its neighbours.

Inside a current-carrying solenoid the magnetic field is strong and uniform: the same strength and direction everywhere inside the coil. It is drawn as straight, evenly spaced, parallel lines running along the axis of the coil.

Outside the coil the field spreads out and has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet, with one end of the solenoid behaving as a north pole and the other as a south pole. The lines outside run from the north end round to the south end, and every line is a closed loop that continues through the inside of the coil.

A core of iron placed inside a solenoid is magnetised by the field of the coil and greatly increases the strength of the magnetic field. Iron is used because it loses almost all of its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core. Its magnetic field can be switched on and off with the current, and its strength can be changed by changing the current or the number of turns.

The magnetic effect of a current is demonstrated by placing plotting compasses, or scattering iron filings, near a wire and switching the current on: the compasses swing round to lie end to end along circles around the wire, and swing back to north when the current is switched off.

The magnetic effect of a current can be increased by increasing the current, by winding the wire into a solenoid with more turns so that the fields of the turns add together, and by adding an iron core.

In a relay a small current in a coil magnetises an iron core, which attracts a pivoted iron armature; the armature closes contacts in a second, separate circuit. A small current can therefore switch on a much larger one, and the two circuits stay electrically isolated from each other.

In an electric bell the current passes through an electromagnet that attracts an iron armature carrying a hammer; as the armature moves it breaks the circuit, the electromagnet switches off, a spring pulls the armature back and the circuit is remade, so the hammer strikes repeatedly.
When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other. This is called the motor effect.

Hold the thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand at right angles to one another. The First finger points along the Field, the seCond finger along the Current, and the thuMb then gives the direction of the force, that is the Motion of the conductor.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the force
concepts.definition: The size of the force on a conductor in a magnetic field depends on the magnetic flux density of the field, the current through the conductor, and the length of conductor that is inside the field.
Magnetic flux density, symbol B, is the measure of the strength of a magnetic field used in this equation. It is measured in tesla, T, and a stronger magnet gives a larger flux density.
For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current: force = magnetic flux density × current × length, written in symbols as F = B I l.
The tesla, T, is the unit of magnetic flux density. A flux density of 1 T gives a force of 1 N on each metre of a conductor carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field.

concepts.term: Symbols and units in F = B I l
concepts.definition: Force, F, in newtons, N; magnetic flux density, B, in tesla, T; current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere); length, l, in metres, m. Values must be substituted in these units, so a length given in centimetres has to be converted to metres first.

A coil of wire carrying a current in a magnetic field tends to rotate, because the forces on its two opposite sides act in opposite directions and so turn the coil about its axle. This is the basis of an electric motor.

The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, just as the coil passes the vertical. The forces on the two sides therefore swap over at the right moment, and the coil keeps rotating in the same direction instead of stopping and rocking back.

misconceptions.question: What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around a long straight current-carrying wire?
misconceptions.correct: The field lines are circles centred on the wire, in a plane at right angles to the wire.
misconceptions.misconception: The field lines point straight outwards from the wire in all directions, like the spokes of a wheel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radial patterns are met first, in diagrams of light spreading from a lamp and of the field around a point charge, and that picture is reused for the wire.
misconceptions.correction: Plotting compasses placed around the wire do not point away from it; they line up end to end and trace closed circles around it. Magnetic field lines are closed loops and never start or end on the wire.

misconceptions.question: In which direction do the magnetic field lines around a straight wire run?
misconceptions.correct: They run around the wire, in circles at right angles to it.
misconceptions.misconception: They run along the wire, in the same direction as the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The current is the only direction marked on the circuit diagram, so the field is assumed to share it.
misconceptions.correction: The field is always at right angles to the current that produces it. A compass held beside the wire turns to lie across the wire, not along it.

misconceptions.question: Does a straight current-carrying wire have a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its field is a set of circles around the wire; poles at the ends belong to a bar magnet or a solenoid.
misconceptions.misconception: The wire behaves like a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every magnet met before this point has two poles, so poles are assumed to be a feature of anything magnetic.
misconceptions.correction: Poles appear where field lines leave and re-enter an object. Around a straight wire the lines simply circle it, so there is nowhere for a pole to be. Winding the wire into a solenoid is what creates ends that act as poles.

misconceptions.question: A compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm from a wire carrying a steady current. What happens to the field at the compass?
misconceptions.correct: The field is weaker, because its strength depends on distance from the wire as well as on the current.
misconceptions.misconception: The field is unchanged, because the current has not changed and current is what sets the field strength.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current is the quantity asked about most often, so distance is treated as scenery rather than as a variable.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the strength of the field depends on the current through the wire AND the distance from the wire. On a field diagram the circles are drawn further apart further out, which is how a weaker field is shown.

misconceptions.question: How far from a current-carrying wire does its magnetic field reach?
misconceptions.correct: The field gets weaker with distance but has no sharp edge; there is no distance at which it suddenly stops.
misconceptions.misconception: The field exists only very close to the wire and stops abruptly at the outermost circle that is drawn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show three or four circles and nothing beyond, so the last circle is read as a boundary.
misconceptions.correction: A diagram can only show a few representative lines. A sensitive compass still deflects well outside the outermost circle drawn; the field fades away gradually.

misconceptions.question: The same wire carrying the same current is wound into a solenoid. What happens to the magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes stronger, because the field of each turn adds to the fields of the turns beside it.
misconceptions.misconception: It becomes weaker, because the current now has a longer path to travel through the coiled wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Longer wire is associated with higher resistance and with things running down, so longer is read as weaker.
misconceptions.correction: Shaping the wire does not use the current up, and the current is set by the circuit. Each turn contributes its own field in the same direction inside the coil, so the fields add and the effect is much stronger.

misconceptions.question: Does a solenoid need an iron core to produce a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: No. A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field on its own; an iron core makes that field stronger.
misconceptions.misconception: A solenoid produces no field at all unless an iron core is placed inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Classroom electromagnets almost always have a core, so the core looks like the part that does the work.
misconceptions.correction: An air-cored solenoid deflects a compass held at its end, showing that a field is already present. The core is magnetised by that field and adds its own, which is why the total field becomes much stronger.

misconceptions.question: What is the magnetic field like inside a current-carrying solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: It is strong and uniform: the same strength and direction throughout the inside of the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: It is strong only at the exact centre of the coil and fades away to nothing elsewhere inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fields met earlier, around a wire or around a pole, weaken with distance from one place, so a single strongest point is expected.
misconceptions.correction: Field lines drawn inside a solenoid are straight, parallel and evenly spaced along its length, which is exactly how a uniform field is shown. Iron filings inside a long coil line up the same way all along it.

misconceptions.question: Which way do the field lines run inside a solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: They run straight along the axis of the coil, from its south end to its north end inside the coil.
misconceptions.misconception: They run in circles around the axis, like the circles around a single straight wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The circular pattern around a straight wire is learned first and is carried over to the coiled wire unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: Each turn does produce circles around its own wire, but inside the coil those circles all point the same way along the axis and add together, while outside them they largely cancel. The result inside is a straight, uniform field.

misconceptions.question: How does the field outside a solenoid compare with the field of a bar magnet?
misconceptions.correct: It has a similar shape, with one end of the coil acting as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no field outside the coil at all, so a solenoid cannot be compared with a bar magnet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emphasis on the strong uniform field inside leads to the outside being ignored, and diagrams often stop at the coil.
misconceptions.correction: Field lines are closed loops, so every line inside the coil must return round the outside. A compass held beyond the end of a solenoid deflects just as it would near the pole of a bar magnet.

misconceptions.question: What happens to an electromagnet when the current is switched off?
misconceptions.correct: The field almost completely disappears, because the iron core keeps very little magnetism.
misconceptions.misconception: The core stays magnetised permanently, so the electromagnet still works with the current switched off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The core is seen becoming a magnet, and permanent magnets are the only kind met before, so the change is assumed to last.
misconceptions.correction: Iron is a soft magnetic material: it magnetises easily and loses that magnetism as soon as the field producing it is removed. Being able to switch the field off is the main advantage of an electromagnet.

misconceptions.question: What does the iron core in an electromagnet do?
misconceptions.correct: It is magnetised by the coil's field and adds its own field, making the total field much stronger.
misconceptions.misconception: The core carries an extra current of its own, and it is this extra current that strengthens the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The core is a piece of metal sitting inside a circuit, so it is assumed to join in as a conductor.
misconceptions.correction: The core is not part of the circuit; the wire wound on it is insulated. It strengthens the field magnetically, by having its own magnetic domains lined up by the coil's field.

misconceptions.question: How can you demonstrate that a current produces a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: Place a plotting compass near the wire and switch the current on: the needle swings away from north.
misconceptions.misconception: A compass placed near the wire deflects only if a permanent magnet is also brought near it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Deflection of a compass is associated with magnets, so a magnet is assumed to be needed before anything can happen.
misconceptions.correction: The whole point of the demonstration is that no magnet is present. The compass swings when the current is switched on and returns to north when it is switched off, so the current alone is producing the field.

misconceptions.question: A wire carrying a current becomes warm. Does this show that it produces a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: No. Warming shows energy transferred by heating; the magnetic effect is shown by a compass deflecting.
misconceptions.misconception: The wire warming up is evidence for the magnetic effect of the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both effects appear when the current is switched on, so any observed change is taken as evidence for whichever effect is being discussed.
misconceptions.correction: A heating effect occurs in any resistor, including ones whose field is far too weak to notice. Only a magnetic test object, such as a plotting compass or iron filings, tests for a magnetic field.

misconceptions.question: Do field lines drawn for a wire or a solenoid need arrows on them?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification asks for the direction of the field to be shown, so every line needs an arrowhead.
misconceptions.misconception: The pattern alone is enough; the arrows are decoration and can be left off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Marks are associated with the shape of the drawing, and direction feels like a detail rather than part of the answer.
misconceptions.correction: A field has a direction at every point, defined as the direction in which a compass north pole points. Without arrows the diagram does not say whether the field runs clockwise or anticlockwise, so it is incomplete.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the field lines at the ends of a solenoid?
misconceptions.correct: They continue out of the end, loop round the outside and re-enter at the other end, forming closed loops.
misconceptions.misconception: The lines start at one end of the coil and stop at the other end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams often show only the inside of the coil, and lines that end at the edge of a drawing look like lines that end.
misconceptions.correction: Magnetic field lines never begin or end anywhere. Continuing each line round the outside is exactly what gives the solenoid its bar-magnet shape and its poles.

misconceptions.question: The current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the field pattern?
misconceptions.correct: The circles stay the same but every arrow points the opposite way round the wire.
misconceptions.misconception: The pattern and the arrows are both unchanged, because the size of the current is the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Field strength is the quantity attended to, and strength does not depend on which way the current flows.
misconceptions.correction: Direction is set by the direction of the current, through the right-hand grip rule. A plotting compass placed by the wire visibly swings through 180° when the connections are swapped over.

misconceptions.question: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?
misconceptions.correct: Because the fields produced by the individual turns point the same way inside the coil and add together.
misconceptions.misconception: Because coiling the wire increases the current flowing through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A stronger effect is equated with more current, since current is the quantity known to control the field.
misconceptions.correction: An ammeter in the circuit shows the current is unchanged, or very slightly smaller because of the extra resistance. What changes is that many turns now contribute their fields at the same place.

misconceptions.question: Does a solenoid work by trapping the magnetic field lines inside the coil?
misconceptions.correct: No. The lines pass out of the ends and loop round outside; the coil concentrates the field, it does not trap it.
misconceptions.misconception: The turns of wire enclose the field so that none of it can escape from the coil.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A container holding something in is an easy way to explain why the field inside is strong.
misconceptions.correction: If nothing escaped there would be no external field and no poles, yet a compass clearly deflects near the end of a solenoid. The field inside is strong because contributions add, not because they are shut in.

misconceptions.question: In a relay, how are the coil circuit and the switched circuit connected?
misconceptions.correct: They are separate circuits; the coil's magnetism moves an armature that closes the contacts of the other one.
misconceptions.misconception: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two circuits are drawn close together on the diagram, and one connected path is the usual picture of a circuit.
misconceptions.correction: Tracing the wires shows that the coil circuit is a complete loop on its own. The only link between the circuits is magnetic, which is why a relay lets a small safe current switch a large one.

misconceptions.question: Does an electromagnet attract or repel the iron armature in a relay or a bell?
misconceptions.correct: It attracts it, because the iron is magnetised so that the end nearest the coil is an opposite pole.
misconceptions.misconception: The electromagnet repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Magnets are remembered as both attracting and repelling, so either seems possible here.
misconceptions.correction: Repulsion needs two magnets with like poles facing. The armature is unmagnetised iron, and induced magnetism always produces an opposite pole facing the magnet, so the force can only be attraction.

misconceptions.question: A current-carrying wire lies in the field of a magnet. Which objects experience a force?
misconceptions.correct: Both do. The magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the wire is pushed; the magnet feels nothing because it is not carrying a current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Only the wire is seen to move in demonstrations, because the magnet is heavy and is usually clamped down.
misconceptions.correction: Forces always come in pairs. The specification says the magnet and the conductor exert a force on each other; stand the magnet on a balance and its reading changes when the current is switched on.

misconceptions.question: In which direction does the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field act?
misconceptions.correct: At right angles to both the current and the field, in the direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
misconceptions.misconception: Along the field lines, in the same direction as the magnetic field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Forces between magnets act along the line joining them, so the force is expected to follow the field here too.
misconceptions.correction: The motor effect force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. Fleming's left-hand rule sets the three directions mutually at right angles, which is why the wire jumps out of the gap rather than along it.

misconceptions.question: Does the force on the conductor act along the wire?
misconceptions.correct: No. It acts at right angles to the wire, so the wire is pushed sideways out of the field.
misconceptions.misconception: The force pushes the wire along its own length, in the direction of the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The current is the most obvious direction in the problem, and a push is assumed to act the way things are already moving.
misconceptions.correction: Fleming's left-hand rule holds the thumb at right angles to the second finger, so the force can never lie along the current. In a demonstration the wire swings sideways across the gap between the poles.

misconceptions.question: Which hand is used for the motor effect?
misconceptions.correct: The left hand. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current-carrying conductor in a field.
misconceptions.misconception: The right hand is used, since the right-hand grip rule was used for the field around a wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Several hand rules are met close together and are stored as one vague hand rule.
misconceptions.correction: The right hand is for the grip rule and for the generator effect; the left hand is for the motor effect. The two hands give opposite answers, so the choice changes the predicted direction.

misconceptions.question: What does each digit represent in Fleming's left-hand rule?
misconceptions.correct: First finger the Field, seCond finger the Current, and the thuMb the force, that is the Motion.
misconceptions.misconception: The first finger is the current and the second finger is the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two fingers look alike and the initial letters are not attached to them, so the pairing is guessed.
misconceptions.correction: The letters are the memory aid: First-Field, seCond-Current, thuMb-Motion. Swapping the two fingers reverses the predicted force, turning a right answer into a wrong one.

misconceptions.question: Which length matters for the size of the force on a conductor?
misconceptions.correct: Only the length of the conductor that is actually inside the magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: The total length of wire in the circuit, including the leads outside the field, sets the size of the force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol l is read simply as length of wire, with no attention paid to which part of it is in the field.
misconceptions.correction: Wire outside the field has no field acting on it, so it contributes no force. Doubling the length of the connecting leads changes nothing; pushing more of the wire between the poles is what increases the force.

misconceptions.question: How can the force on a conductor in a magnetic field be made larger?
misconceptions.correct: Increase the current, use a magnet of larger flux density, or put more of the conductor in the field.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduce the current so that less energy is wasted heating the wire, leaving more available for the force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy-saving language from earlier electricity work is imported into a question about the size of a force.
misconceptions.correction: F = B I l says the force is proportional to the current, so reducing the current reduces the force. Heating is a separate effect and takes nothing away from the magnetic force.

misconceptions.question: What is the force on a conductor that lies along the magnetic field lines?
misconceptions.correct: Zero. The equation applies to a conductor at right angles to the field, and a wire along the field feels no force.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is largest then, because the wire is lined up with the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lined up sounds like the best possible arrangement, as it is when two magnets attract each other.
misconceptions.correction: The motor effect force is perpendicular to both the current and the field, and no such direction exists when the two are parallel. Turning the wire until it is at right angles to the field gives the largest force.

misconceptions.question: What is the equation for the force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field?
misconceptions.correct: force = magnetic flux density × current × length.
misconceptions.misconception: force = magnetic flux density × charge × length, using charge in place of current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Charge and current both describe the flow of electrons and are treated as interchangeable words.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity in the equation is current, measured in amperes, not charge measured in coulombs. Substituting a charge gives an answer that is not in newtons, which is a quick check on the mistake.

misconceptions.question: In F = B I l, what does the symbol B stand for?
misconceptions.correct: The magnetic flux density of the field, measured in tesla.
misconceptions.misconception: The number of magnetic field lines drawn on the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams show more lines for a stronger field, so the count of lines is taken to be the quantity itself.
misconceptions.correction: The number of lines drawn is a choice made by whoever drew the diagram. Flux density is a measured quantity in tesla, shown by how closely the lines are spaced rather than by how many are drawn.

misconceptions.question: In F = B I l, what does the symbol l stand for?
misconceptions.correct: The length of the conductor that is in the magnetic field, in metres.
misconceptions.misconception: The length of the whole circuit, measured all the way round from the cell and back again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The letter l is read as length, with no thought given to which length is meant.
misconceptions.correction: Only conductor inside the field contributes to the force. In a calculation the value substituted is the length of wire lying between the poles of the magnet, converted into metres.

misconceptions.question: What quantity is B, and what is its unit?
misconceptions.correct: B is the magnetic flux density, measured in tesla, T.
misconceptions.misconception: B is the strength of the magnet's pull, measured in newtons, N.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Strength is associated with force, and force is the only magnetic quantity with a familiar unit, so the loose phrase magnetic field strength is used and given newtons.
misconceptions.correction: Force is measured in newtons; magnetic flux density is measured in tesla. In F = B I l the newtons appear on the left of the equation, produced by tesla × amperes × metres on the right.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of the current in F = B I l?
misconceptions.correct: The ampere, A; amp is acceptable for ampere.
misconceptions.misconception: The volt, V, because the supply is what drives the circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Voltage is the number written on the power supply, so it is the electrical quantity most readily recalled.
misconceptions.correction: Current is measured in amperes and read on an ammeter placed in series with the conductor. The potential difference does not appear anywhere in this equation.

misconceptions.question: A wire of length 30 cm is in a magnetic field. What value of l is substituted into F = B I l?
misconceptions.correct: 0.30 m, because the length must be substituted in metres.
misconceptions.misconception: 30, using the number exactly as it is given in centimetres.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number is copied straight from the question without checking it against the unit list for the equation.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives length, l, in metres, m. Substituting centimetres makes the answer 100 times too large, which is usually obvious when the answer is compared with everyday forces.

misconceptions.question: The force, current and length are known. How is the magnetic flux density found?
misconceptions.correct: Rearrange to B = F ÷ (I × l) and divide the force by the product of current and length.
misconceptions.misconception: Multiply the three known values together, because the equation contains multiplication signs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as a set of numbers to multiply rather than as a relation that has to be rearranged.
misconceptions.correction: B sits on the right-hand side of F = B I l, so it has to be made the subject first. Multiplying instead of dividing normally gives an answer far too large, which is worth checking.

misconceptions.question: Why does a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field rotate?
misconceptions.correct: The current runs opposite ways along the two sides, so the forces on them act in opposite directions.
misconceptions.misconception: The forces on the two sides act in the same direction, so the whole coil is pushed round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fleming's rule is applied once and the answer is reused for the whole coil, without noticing that the current has turned round.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the current round the loop: along one side it flows one way and along the opposite side it flows back. The second finger points opposite ways for the two sides, so one is pushed up while the other is pushed down, and that pair of forces turns the coil.

misconceptions.question: Does the coil in a motor rotate because it is attracted to one of the magnet's poles?
misconceptions.correct: No. It rotates because of the motor-effect forces on its current-carrying sides.
misconceptions.misconception: The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled bodily towards the north pole of the magnet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Attraction between poles is the familiar magnetic explanation and is reached for before the motor effect is considered.
misconceptions.correction: The coil turns on a fixed axle and does not move towards either pole. What acts on it is a pair of equal forces in opposite directions on opposite sides, which produces rotation and no overall pull.

misconceptions.question: What is the job of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor?
misconceptions.correct: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn so that the coil keeps turning the same way.
misconceptions.misconception: Its only job is to carry the current into the coil so that a force can act on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The commutator is where the current enters, so its contact role is noticed and its switching role is missed.
misconceptions.correction: Plain slip rings would also carry the current in, and the coil would then stop and rock back after half a turn. The split in the ring is what swaps the connections at that moment and keeps the rotation going.

misconceptions.question: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is clamped so that it cannot move. Is there a force on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The force acts whether or not the wire is free to move; clamping it simply stops it accelerating.
misconceptions.misconception: There is no force until the wire is released and allowed to move about.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force is identified with visible movement, so a stationary object is assumed to have no force on it.
misconceptions.correction: A clamped wire pushes on its clamp, and a magnet resting on a balance shows a change in reading when the current flows. The force is present; the wire is simply held in place by a second force.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities must be substituted when F = B I l is used?
misconceptions.correct: All three: the flux density, the current and the length of conductor in the field.
misconceptions.misconception: Two of them are enough, so one quantity is quietly left out of the working.
misconceptions.whyItArises: With three numbers to combine, one is dropped as the calculation is written down, especially when two of them multiply neatly.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation out, then substitute the numbers in the same order as the symbols. Checking that the units multiply to give newtons catches a missing quantity straight away.

misconceptions.question: What is it that reverses every half turn in a simple d.c. motor?
misconceptions.correct: The direction of the current in the coil, reversed by the split-ring commutator.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnetic field reverses every half turn while the current stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Something clearly has to reverse for the coil to keep turning, and the field is the other direction in the problem.
misconceptions.correction: The field comes from a fixed permanent magnet and cannot reverse. The split ring turns with the coil and swaps which brush feeds which side, so it is the current in the coil that reverses.

mcqs.stem: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current. What is the shape of the magnetic field pattern around the wire?

options.text: Circles centred on the wire and lying in a plane at right angles to it
options.rationale: The field around a straight current-carrying wire is a set of concentric circles perpendicular to it.

options.text: Straight lines that spread out from the wire, like spokes on a wheel
options.rationale: A student picturing a radial pattern, as for light from a lamp, draws lines pointing away from the wire.

options.text: Straight lines running parallel to the wire along its whole length
options.rationale: A student who gives the field the same direction as the current draws it along the wire.

options.text: Loops that leave one end of the wire and enter at the other end
options.rationale: This is the bar-magnet pattern, which belongs to a solenoid and not to one straight wire.

mcqs.stem: A plotting compass is moved from 2 cm to 6 cm away from a wire carrying a steady current. The current is not changed. What happens to the deflection of the compass?

options.text: It stays the same, because the current through the wire is unchanged
options.rationale: A student who treats the current as the only factor ignores the distance named in the specification.

options.text: It falls to zero, because the field stops at the outer circle
options.rationale: A student who reads the outermost circle of a diagram as an edge expects the field to end there.

options.text: It gets smaller, because the field is weaker further from the wire
options.rationale: Field strength depends on distance from the wire as well as on the current, so it falls as the compass is moved away.

options.text: It gets larger, because the field circles are wider further out
options.rationale: Wider circles are more widely spaced, which shows a weaker field, but size is read here as strength.

mcqs.stem: A student winds a straight wire into a solenoid and passes the same current through it as before. What happens to the magnetic field produced?

options.text: It is weaker, because the current now has a longer path to run
options.rationale: A student who links extra length with extra resistance expects the coiled wire to give a weaker field.

options.text: It is stronger, because the fields of the turns add together
options.rationale: Shaping a wire into a solenoid increases the strength of the field, because each turn adds its field to its neighbours'.

options.text: It is unchanged, because the current in the wire is unchanged
options.rationale: A student who treats the current as the only thing that matters sees no reason for the shape to count.

options.text: There is no field at all until an iron core is in the coil
options.rationale: A student who has only seen cored electromagnets thinks the core is what creates the field.

mcqs.stem: What best describes the magnetic field inside a long solenoid that is carrying a current?

options.text: Strong at the very centre of the coil and almost zero elsewhere
options.rationale: A student who expects every field to fade with distance from one point looks for a single strongest place.

options.text: A set of circles running round the axis, as around a straight wire
options.rationale: A student who carries the straight-wire pattern into the coil keeps the circles inside it.

options.text: Weak inside the coil and strongest just outside the windings
options.rationale: A student who thinks the field is squeezed out of the coil puts the strong region outside it.

options.text: Strong and uniform, drawn as evenly spaced parallel lines
options.rationale: The specification states that the field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform, so the lines are parallel and evenly spaced.

mcqs.stem: How does the magnetic field around the outside of a current-carrying solenoid compare with that of a bar magnet?

options.text: It is a set of circles around the middle of the coil, not like a bar magnet
options.rationale: A student still using the straight-wire pattern wraps circles round the body of the coil.

options.text: It has a similar shape, with one end acting as a north pole and one as a south
options.rationale: The specification states that the field around a solenoid has a similar shape to that of a bar magnet.

options.text: It has exactly the same shape, but the ends of a solenoid are not poles
options.rationale: A student who reserves the word pole for permanent magnets denies the solenoid any poles.

options.text: There is no field outside the coil, so no comparison can be made
options.rationale: A student who has only met the strong uniform field inside forgets that the lines must return outside.

mcqs.stem: An iron core is placed inside a solenoid that is carrying a current. What is the effect?

options.text: The solenoid begins to produce a magnetic field for the first time
options.rationale: A student who thinks the core creates the field believes there was nothing there before.

options.text: The field grows stronger and stays on after the current is off
options.rationale: A student who treats the magnetised core as a permanent magnet expects the field to remain.

options.text: The core carries a current of its own that adds to the field
options.rationale: A student who sees a metal core inside a circuit assumes it must conduct as well.

options.text: The magnetic field of the solenoid becomes considerably stronger
options.rationale: Adding an iron core increases the strength of the magnetic field of a solenoid; the arrangement is an electromagnet.

mcqs.stem: Which observation best demonstrates that a current in a wire produces a magnetic field?

options.text: A compass beside the wire swings round when the current is switched on
options.rationale: The compass responds only to a magnetic field, and it moves exactly when the current begins, so the current is the cause.

options.text: A plotting compass beside the wire keeps pointing north when the current is off
options.rationale: A student who expects a magnet to be needed reports the ordinary behaviour of a compass as the result.

options.text: The wire becomes noticeably warmer when the current is switched on
options.rationale: A student who accepts any change caused by the current offers the heating effect as evidence.

options.text: A piece of copper wire placed beside the wire is pulled sideways towards it
options.rationale: A student who thinks all metals are magnetic predicts an attraction that does not happen.

mcqs.stem: The direction of the current in a straight wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field pattern?

options.text: The pattern and the arrows on it are both completely unchanged
options.rationale: A student attending only to the size of the current sees no reason for anything to reverse.

options.text: The circles turn into straight lines pointing back along the wire
options.rationale: A student who ties the field direction to the current direction redraws the whole pattern.

options.text: The circles stay, but the arrows point the other way round
options.rationale: The pattern is fixed by the shape of the wire and the direction by the direction of the current, so only the arrows reverse.

options.text: The circles are replaced by a bar-magnet pattern with swapped poles
options.rationale: A student who thinks the wire has poles reverses those poles instead of the arrows.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to draw the magnetic field of a current-carrying solenoid, showing its direction. Which drawing is correct?

options.text: Parallel lines inside the coil and loops outside it, with no arrows on any line
options.rationale: A student who thinks the pattern alone earns the marks leaves the direction off the diagram.

options.text: Parallel arrows inside the coil that start at one end and stop at the other
options.rationale: A student who ignores the outside of the coil lets the field lines start and finish at the ends.

options.text: Closely spaced parallel arrows inside the coil, looping outside from north to south
options.rationale: Inside the coil the field is uniform and along the axis; outside, each line loops back, giving the bar-magnet shape.

options.text: Circles drawn around the outside of the coil, with clockwise arrows shown
options.rationale: A student reusing the straight-wire pattern wraps circles round the body of the solenoid.

mcqs.stem: Why does winding a wire into a solenoid increase the magnetic effect of the current?

options.text: The field of each turn points the same way inside the coil, so they add up
options.rationale: Many turns contribute their fields at the same place and in the same direction, so the total field is much stronger.

options.text: Winding the wire into a coil increases the current flowing in it
options.rationale: A student who links a stronger effect only with a bigger current invents an increase in current.

options.text: The coiled wire has a much larger resistance, and that strengthens the field
options.rationale: A student who remembers that coils have resistance treats resistance as the cause of the field.

options.text: The turns of wire trap the field lines so that none can escape the coil
options.rationale: A student using a container picture explains the strong inside field by shutting the field in.

mcqs.stem: A relay diagram shows a coil wound on an iron core in one circuit, and a pivoted iron armature that closes contacts in a second circuit. How does the relay work?

options.text: The current in the coil flows on through the contacts and into the second circuit
options.rationale: A student who reads the touching contacts as a join treats the two circuits as one.

options.text: The magnetised iron core repels the armature and pushes it onto the contacts
options.rationale: A student who expects magnets to repel as readily as attract chooses a push rather than a pull.

options.text: The coil heats the armature, which bends until it touches the contacts
options.rationale: A student thinking of a bimetallic strip in a thermostat applies a heating explanation here.

options.text: A small current magnetises the core, so the armature closes the contacts
options.rationale: The coil's magnetic effect moves the armature, so a small current in one circuit switches on a separate circuit.

mcqs.stem: A wire carrying a current is held at right angles to the field between the poles of a magnet. Which statement about the forces is correct?

options.text: Only the wire feels a force, as the magnet carries no current
options.rationale: A student who watches only the wire move concludes that the magnet is not involved.

options.text: The magnet and the wire each exert a force on the other
options.rationale: The specification states that the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on each other.

options.text: Only the magnet feels a force, because it produces the field
options.rationale: A student who treats the field's owner as the active object puts the force on the magnet alone.

options.text: Neither feels a force until the wire is free to move about
options.rationale: A student who identifies force with visible movement denies a force to a clamped wire.

mcqs.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what do the first finger, the second finger and the thumb represent?

options.text: The first finger is the current, the second the field, the thumb the motion
options.rationale: A student who remembers two fingers but not which is which swaps the field and the current.

options.text: The first finger is the force, the second the field, and the thumb current
options.rationale: A student who puts the force on a finger rather than the thumb reorders all three.

options.text: The right hand is used, with the field, current and force in that order
options.rationale: A student who has met the right-hand grip rule uses the same hand for the motor effect.

options.text: The first finger the field, the second finger the current, and the thumb the force
options.rationale: First finger Field, seCond finger Current, thuMb Motion: the three are held at right angles to one another.

mcqs.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current from left to right. The magnetic field between the poles is directed into the page. In which direction is the force on the wire?

options.text: Downwards, at right angles to both the field and the current
options.rationale: A student who swaps the first and second fingers gets a force in exactly the opposite direction.

options.text: Upwards, at right angles to both the current and the field
options.rationale: First finger into the page and second finger to the right puts the thumb, and so the force, upwards.

options.text: Into the page, in the same direction as the field itself
options.rationale: A student who expects magnetic forces to act along the field lines pushes the wire along them.

options.text: To the right, in the same direction as the current
options.rationale: A student who assumes a push acts the way the current flows sends the wire along its own length.

mcqs.stem: Which change would increase the size of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?

options.text: Using much longer connecting leads between the cell and the wire
options.rationale: A student who reads l as the length of wire in the circuit adds length outside the field.

options.text: Using a much longer wire, most of it outside the field
options.rationale: Believing total wire length (including parts outside the field) sets the force, so a longer wire seems to increase it; really only length within the field counts in F=BIL.

options.text: Using a stronger magnet, so that the flux density is larger
options.rationale: The force depends on the magnetic flux density, the current and the length of conductor in the field.

options.text: Reducing the current so that less energy is lost as heat
options.rationale: A student importing energy-saving language treats a smaller current as more effective.

mcqs.stem: A straight wire carrying a current is placed so that it lies along the magnetic field lines. What is the force on the wire?

options.text: Zero, because the wire is not at right angles to the field
options.rationale: The equation applies to a conductor at right angles to the field; a wire lying along the field feels no force.

options.text: The largest possible force, as the wire lies along the field
options.rationale: A student who reads 'lined up' as the ideal arrangement expects the biggest force there.

options.text: Exactly the same force as when the wire is at right angles to it
options.rationale: A student who treats the equation as always applying ignores the condition attached to it.

options.text: A force along the wire, in the direction of the current in it
options.rationale: A student who has the force following the current keeps it along the wire.

mcqs.stem: For a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field and carrying a current, which word equation gives the force on the conductor?

options.text: force = magnetic field strength × current × length
options.rationale: A student who thinks of B as the pull of the magnet uses the loose phrase instead of flux density.

options.text: force = magnetic flux density × charge × length
options.rationale: A student who treats charge and current as the same quantity puts charge into the equation.

options.text: force = magnetic flux density × current × length
options.rationale: This is the equation as the specification states it, for a conductor at right angles to the field.

options.text: force = magnetic flux density × current × time
options.rationale: A student who half-remembers the equation replaces the length with the more familiar time.

mcqs.stem: In the equation F = B I l, what do the symbols B and l stand for?

options.text: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of conductor in the field
options.rationale: B is the flux density in tesla and l is the length of the conductor that lies inside the field, in metres.

options.text: B is the magnetic flux density and l is the length of the whole circuit
options.rationale: A student who reads l as simply 'length of wire' counts the leads outside the field as well.

options.text: B is the number of field lines drawn and l is the length of the wire
options.rationale: A student who reads flux density off a diagram counts lines instead of measuring in tesla.

options.text: B is the force from the magnet and l is the length of the conductor
options.rationale: A student who confuses the cause with the field itself makes B a force in newtons.

mcqs.stem: Which set of units should be used when the equation F = B I l is applied?

options.text: F in newtons, B in newtons, I in amperes and l in metres
options.rationale: A student who treats flux density as the pull of the magnet gives it the unit of force.

options.text: F in newtons, B in tesla, I in volts and l in centimetres
options.rationale: A student who recalls the supply voltage rather than the current also leaves the length in centimetres.

options.text: F in joules, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
options.rationale: A student who confuses force with the energy transferred writes the force in joules.

options.text: F in newtons, B in tesla, I in amperes and l in metres
options.rationale: These are the units given in the specification: force in newtons, flux density in tesla, current in amperes, length in metres.

mcqs.stem: A wire of length 0.30 m lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. The current in the wire is 2.0 A. What is the force on the wire?

options.rationale: A student who mishandles the decimal point in 0.20 × 0.30 arrives at an answer ten times too small.
F = B I l = 0.20 × 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.12 N, with the length already in metres.
A student who leaves the length out of the calculation works out only 0.20 × 2.0.
A student who substitutes the length as 30 cm gets an answer one hundred times too large.

mcqs.stem: A wire of length 0.30 m carries a current of 8.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on the wire is 4.8 N. What is the magnetic flux density?

options.rationale: Rearranging gives B = F ÷ (I × l) = 4.8 ÷ (8.0 × 0.30) = 2.0 T.
A student who multiplies all three given values together instead of rearranging gets 4.8 × 8.0 × 0.30.
A student who substitutes the length as 30 rather than 0.30 divides by a number 100 times too big.
A student who divides the force by the length alone and forgets the current gets 4.8 ÷ 0.30.

mcqs.stem: A rectangular coil carrying a current is mounted on an axle between the poles of a magnet. Why does the coil tend to rotate?

options.text: The forces on both of its sides act in the same direction, pushing it
options.rationale: A student who applies Fleming's rule once and reuses the answer gets two forces the same way.

options.text: The coil becomes a magnet and is pulled towards the north pole
options.rationale: A student explaining everything by attraction between poles predicts a pull rather than a turn.

options.text: The forces on its opposite sides act in opposite directions
options.rationale: The current runs opposite ways along the two sides, so the forces on them are opposite and turn the coil.

options.text: The current warms the coil, which expands and turns on its axle
options.rationale: A student falling back on the heating effect of a current invents a thermal cause for the motion.

mcqs.stem: In a simple d.c. motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?

options.text: It carries the current into the coil, so that a force can act on the coil
options.rationale: A student who notices only where the current enters describes the contact and misses the switching.

options.text: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so it keeps turning one way
options.rationale: Swapping the connections as the coil passes the vertical swaps the two forces over and keeps the rotation going.

options.text: It reverses the magnetic field every half turn, so the coil keeps going
options.rationale: A student who knows something must reverse picks the field, which is fixed by the permanent magnet.

options.text: It holds the coil steady so that it turns at a constant rate of spin
options.rationale: A student who associates the ring with smooth running gives it a speed-control job.
